briefs.headline: Daily power demand rises to 290 MU in Andhra Pradesh, says Energy Minister Ravi Kumar
briefs.deck: Apart from increasing power generation by AP-Genco, additional electricity is being procured through other sources to ensure uninterrupted supply, he says
briefs.bodyText:
Andhra Pradesh’s daily electricity requirement has increased from 265 MU to 290 MU, says Energy Minister Gottipati Ravi Kumar.
The Minister, along with MLA Damacharla Janardhana Rao, inaugurated a 132/33 kV AP-Transco substation constructed at a cost of ₹44.25 crore at Kothapatnam in Ongole Assembly constituency on Thursday.
Addressing the media later, Mr. Ravi Kumar said, “To meet the rising demand, power generation by AP-Genco is being increased. This apart, additional electricity is being procured through other sources. The government is ensuring uninterrupted supply despite the increase in demand and will accelerate infrastructure development to meet future requirements.”
“The State is expanding its power infrastructure to meet the growing demand for electricity. The government is strengthening the power network in the rural and urban areas through construction of substations, installation of transformers and feeders, replacement of poles and old conductors, and laying of new power lines wherever required,” the Minister said.
Mr. Ravi Kumar further said that AP-Transco was investing around ₹6,000 crore for the construction of substations across the State.
“In Prakasam district alone, 11 substations have already been constructed, while another seven are under construction,” he added.
The Minister alleged that the power sector had suffered neglect during the YSRCP government’s term between 2019 and 2024. He said that several substations, for which land had been identified and funds made available, were not taken up by the YSRCP administration.
The Minister also inaugurated a Skill Development Centre in Ongole, besides opening a Centre of Excellence focused on skill training in electric vehicles, drone technology and other emerging technologies. He later reviewed the preparations for Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu’s public meeting scheduled for Friday.

briefs.headline: Madras High Court permits observance of first death anniversary of prime accused Nagendran in BSP leader Armstrong murder case
briefs.deck: Justice V. Lakshminarayanan permitted the event to take place at Vysarpadi in Chennai on October 9, 2026
briefs.bodyText:
The Madras High Court on Thursday (October 8, 2026) directed the Greater Chennai City Police to grant permission for the observance of the first death anniversary of P. Nagendran, who was the prime accused in the July 2024 murder of former Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) leader K. Armstrong, on Friday (October 9, 2026).
Justice V. Lakshminarayanan quashed an order passed by the police denying permission for the event since they apprehended disturbance to law and order due to possible retaliatory action. He directed them to grant conditional permission by imposing reasonable restrictions such as limiting the number of participants.
Though Nagendran’s family had initially sought permission for the participation of 300 members in the event planned to be conducted at their residence in Vyasarpadi, they agreed to restrict the number of participants to 60 and submit the list of names to the police by Friday morning.
The judge also made it clear the event should be conducted between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m. at the Vysarpadi residence of the family by singing threnodies (oppari), beating drums (parai) and serving food (annadhanam) as per the customs of the community to which they belonged.
He recorded the submission of the counsel for Nagendran’s wife that there shall not be any political sloganeering, erection of banners or playing of provocative songs during the event. The judge took note that Nagendran had died in judicial custody in connection with multiple criminal cases.
“This court is of the view that eventhough the deceased happens to be one of the fakest villains of the 21st century, his family is entitled to follow the customary observances in line with their beliefs. The accused is dead but his family members are alive. The petitioner fears if such observances are not followed, the family will be inviting disastrous consequences from their forefathers. Sometimes, rationality cannot be attached to beliefs,” the judge wrote.
On the apprehension of Additional Public Prosecutor Arun Anbumani that the deceased was the prime accused in the brutal murder of a leading political personality in the State and hence there could be a retaliation, especially since the son of the deceased was also an accused in the murder case, the judge said, the Tamil Nadu police was robust enough to ensure nothing untoward takes place during the three-hour event.
He ordered that the participants must not consume liquor and the police could intervene if there was violation of any of the conditions imposed by the court.

briefs.headline: Madras High Court Registry lodges police complaint for forging its proceedings to get Bangladesh nationals deported
briefs.deck: Justice V. Lakshminarayanan has directed the police to investigate the matter and submit a status report by November 10, 2026
briefs.bodyText:
The Madras High Court Registry has lodged a complaint with the Greater Chennai Commissioner of Police in connection with its proceedings having been forged to get five Bangladesh nationals, lodged in a special foreigners camp at Attur in Salem district, deported to their country.
Appearing before Justice V. Lakshminarayanan, the High Court’s standing counsel S. John Raja Singh reported that a complaint on behalf of the Registrar General Deepthi Arivunithi was lodged with the Chennai city police on Tuesday (October 6, 2026) in compliance of the court orders.
Bilal alias Mohammed Bilal Syed, Y. Salim and Bimal Sutrada alias Laxman Das had filed three individual writ petitions in the High Court seeking a direction to the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) in Chennai as well as the State police to take steps for deporting them to their country.
Substantiating their claim, the petitioners had submitted copies of official proceedings supposedly issued by the Registrar (Judicial) of the High Court on October 8, 2025 granting clearance for deportation of five Bangladesh nationals to their home country and insisted that they must be sent back forthwith.
Shocked to come across such proceedings, Justice Lakshminarayanan had on September 1, 2026 directed the High Court Registry to verify whether it had issued any such proceedings. The Registrar (Judicial) submitted a report on September 8, 2026 stating it was a forged document.
Additional Public Prosecutor Arun Anbumani told the court the petitioners had also annexed a document purportedly issued in favour of them by the Director General of Prisons and Correctional Services but the officer had confirmed that no such document had been issued by his office.
Central government standing counsel M.P. Jaisha, representing the FRRO, told the court that a complaint regarding forgery of government documents had already been lodged with the Central Crime Branch police in 2025 and that a First Information Report too was registered.
After recording their submissions, the judge had directed the High Court Registry to lodge a police complaint with regard to forgery of its proceedings. On being told the complaint was lodged on October 6, the judge called for a status report from the police by November 10, 2026.

briefs.headline: Retired Assam Forest officer’s extension in key post challenged
briefs.deck: The Gauhati High Court has sought a response from the State government in the second petition in about a month
briefs.bodyText:
The Gauhati High Court has issued notices to the Assam government and other respondents after admitting a petition challenging the legal authority under which retired Indian Forest Service officer M.K. Yadava was reappointed as Special Chief Secretary (Forest) with “full financial and administrative powers”.
Filed on Monday (October 5, 2026), activist Amarjyoti Choudhury’s petition was the second in about a month. In September, the High Court issued a similar notice after hearing a petition by eastern Assam-based conservationist Rohit Choudhury, citing the Union Environment Ministry’s adverse observations against Mr Yadava in the past.
Amarjyoti Choudhury’s petition, filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, does not challenge the government’s power to engage retired officials contractually. Instead, it asks whether a retired officer appointed on contract can be vested with substantive governmental powers ordinarily exercised under the State’s statutory, administrative and financial framework.
He argued that “full financial and administrative powers” vested in Mr Yadava cannot, by itself, constitute a blanket delegation of every financial and administrative power available within the department. The petition seeks disclosure of the precise legal instrument, delegation or government order through which those powers were vested in him.
The petition also cited government records showing Mr Yadava’s involvement in operational and inter-departmental matters, including directions on district survey reports, mining-related regulatory issues and other departmental matters.
Mr Yadava retired from service on February 29, 2024, after serving as Assam’s Principal Chief Conservator of Forests and Head of Forest Force. He was appointed as the Special Chief Secretary (Forest) on March 1, 2024, and his tenure was extended twice—first in February 2025 and then on May 14. His current tenure ends on November 12.
The High Court set November 4 as the next hearing date.
Kaziranga ESZ
On September 29, Rohit Choudhury wrote to Assam Chief Secretary Ravi Kota seeking immediate and authoritative clarification on the legal basis of statements on the extent of the Eco-Sensitive Zone (ESZ) around Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve and restrictions on construction within the zone.
Mr Choudhury referred to Assam Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Jayanta Mallabaruah’s view on X that the ESZ extends 1-3 km from the park’s boundary according to the Supreme Court guidelines and that indigenous communities cannot build their homes due to restrictions.
The environmentalist sought clarification on the legal instruments supporting these assertions, arguing that the apex court’s directions need to be read alongside subsequent orders and the applicable ESZ notification for the protected area.
He cited the Supreme Court’s June 3, 2022, judgment that prescribes a minimum 1 km ESZ from the demarcated boundary of each protected area. He also pointed to the apex court’s April 26, 2023, order, which states that ESZs cannot be uniform and must be specific to individual protected areas.

stories.headline: Car crashes into petrol pump, catches fire near Attibele in Bengaluru
stories.deck: According to police, the driver was travelling with a young woman when he allegedly lost control of the car and hit a petrol pump employee before crashing into the fuel dispensing unit
stories.bodyText:
A high-end car allegedly driven at high speed rammed into a petrol pump at Attibele on the outskirts of Bengaluru, triggering a fire leading to panic among customers and staff.
The incident occurred at an HP petrol station near the Attibele border with Tamil Nadu. According to police, the driver, identified as Sanjay, was travelling with a young woman when he allegedly lost control of the car and hit petrol pump employee Guddu Kumar before crashing into the petrol dispensing unit.
The vehicle and the pump caught fire, and the flames spread within seconds.
Sanjay and the woman managed to get out of the car before it was engulfed in flames. Guddu Kumar sustained serious injuries to his leg and was shifted to a private hospital, where he is undergoing treatment.
One fire tender each from Electronics City and Anekal, and one from Hosur in Tamil Nadu rushed to the spot and brought the blaze under control.
Attibele police have taken Sanjay into custody and registered a case. Further investigation is under way.

stories.headline: Bengaluru police ease CJP’s path for Tiranga march with conditions
stories.deck: In India, Bengaluru Was The First Place To Allow Tiranga March: CJP’s South Coordinator
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Police met Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) Karnataka state committee halfway Friday, allowing its planned ‘tiranga march’ in the city but imposing restrictions on raising slogans and placards.
The march, organised jointly by CJP and Jagruta Karnataka, was taken out to protest the detention of several youngsters for unfurling the Indian flag and to demand electoral reforms and the release of protesters detained in Delhi. Hundreds of Bengalureans, including students, activists and CJP members, gathered at Puttanna Chetty Town Hall around 4.30pm, holding the tricolour and raising patriotic slogans.
They marched to Quit India Memorial on Kempegowda Road, despite persistent rain. While reports suggested that permission had been denied, cops had granted approval subject to several conditions.
These included a ban on protest slogans during the march, slogans against any political party, organisation, community or individual, and the display of protest placards at the concluding venue. Cops also warned that violations could invite legal action, citing a Karnataka high court order restricting protests, processions and similar activities in Bengaluru to Freedom Park.
Before the march, participants demanded the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the withdrawal of SIR of electoral rolls. A major demand was the release of CJP leaders Ashutosh Ranka, Saurav Das and Abhijeet Dipke.
“Many of us here are worried about the situation in the country, and this is more of a march to protect our rights. Many have come without any affiliation to an organisation, as it is important for this resistance not to be centred around Delhi. Not just urban areas, even rural areas have been affected significantly,” said Avani Choksi, a lawyer.
At Quit India Memorial, participants wrapped the pillar in tricolour flags and recited poems. “The whole narrative is not about whether we can march in Bengaluru. We’ve done this before and will do it again. The main part of the struggle is that both SIR and Gyanesh have to go,” said Clifton D’Rozario, a CPI(ML) central committee member.
CJP’s south zone coordinator Bhavana said, “We’re very happy that, as a group, we could pull off such a march. Though there were initial setbacks, police supported us throughout the evening. In India, Bengaluru is the first place where we were able to conduct a tiranga march.”
For many young participants, frustration with the Centre was the principal reason for joining the march. “The tricolour means unity. When govt calls us anti-national, we want to say that we love our country and want to protect its democracy at any cost... I think more such gatherings will happen in the coming months,” said Pavel Pandit, one such participant.
Before dispersing, the organisers sang K’naan’s ‘Wavin’ Flag’ and recited the national anthem, even as rain continued and restrictions remained in force.
No traffic Disruption
Despite hundreds marching through the heart of Bengaluru on a working day, there was little to no traffic disruption during peak traffic hours. Across the entirety of the tiranga march, dozens of khaki-clad officers held ropes creating boundaries between the marching citizens and traffic. Despite heavy police deployment and continuous surveillance, the participants and police did not have major clashes. Media personnel were barred from entering the Quit India Memorial until all participants had entered the spot.
However, once the march culminated at Quit India Memorial, several participants alleged that mufti-clad police officers had intervened when they chanted slogans. While the issue was resolved quickly, several lawyers reiterated that officers should identify issues before carrying out their duties. “Those in mufti should just observe,” a participant was heard shouting.
The crowds were dispersed at around 6pm.
ABVP awareness against anti-SIR protests
BJP-backed student organisation Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) Friday evening held an awareness gathering against the nationwide anti-SIR protests. “In our country, certain anti-social organisations are attempting to create anarchy; we strongly object to this,” ABVP said. The gathering, which was hosted near Jayanagar Ganapathi Temple, drew several members from right-wing organisations who protested against CJP as well. “CJP and opposition parties are trying to bring regime change through undemocratic ways. If somebody wants to bring regime change, it should be through democratic ways; we oppose these protests,” Abhinandan Mirji, ABVP Bengaluru’s Mahanagara secretary, told 
TOI.

stories.headline: SIR in Karnataka: Just 9% of deleted voters apply to return
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: Just 10.07 lakh Form 6 applications for inclusion in 
Karnataka
’s electoral rolls have been received since the rolls were frozen on June 16 for the special intensive revision (SIR) — barely 9% of the 1.07 crore voters struck off the draft rolls under the ASDDO (absent, shifted, dead or duplicate) category.
For voters deleted under ASDDO, filing Form 6 as a new voter was the only route back onto the rolls before the claims and objections deadline of Sept 23. Of the total applications received, 7.86 lakh came in before the deadline, chief electoral officer Anbu Kumar had said earlier. Once verified and processed, these applicants will also be included in the final SIR rolls.
However, the number of applicants who were actually deleted under ASDDO remains unknown. An official from the CEO’s office said Friday that this couldn’t be calculated because the database was now with the Election Commission of India (ECI), and the state office no longer had access to it. The 9% figure, therefore, overstates the recovery, as Form 6 is also used by first-time voters never on the rolls.
Uneven recovery
CEO data available until Oct 16 showed wide variations across districts. Udupi, at 26.3%, was the only district where Form 6 applications exceeded 25% of ASDDO deletions. 
It was followed by Dakshina Kannada (23.6%), Uttara Kannada (18.2%), Chikkamagaluru (16.3%), and Tumakuru (16.1%).
Bengaluru is likely to have the lowest replacement rate. Form 6 applications amounted to just 4.6% of ASDDO deletions in BBMP South, 5.6% in BBMP Central, and 6.1% in BBMP North. Bellary recorded 6.6% and Bengaluru Urban, 6.7%.
Mop-up planned
Form 6 has been made available to all voters not enrolled elsewhere, including those in the ASDDO category. The CEO’s office plans a mop-up exercise after the final SIR rolls are published on Oct 27 to enrol voters who were missed.
With the final rolls due in days, the low return rate — particularly in Bengaluru’s urban constituencies — is likely to draw scrutiny over how many eligible voters may be left out of the revised list.

briefs.headline: Karnataka Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar cautions Ministers against possible ‘sting operations’
briefs.deck: Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar is learnt to have warned his Cabinet colleagues to remain vigilant against possible sting operations, amid reports that private agencies could be secretly recording Ministers’ conversations, meetings, and movements
briefs.bodyText:
Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar is learnt to have warned his Cabinet colleagues to remain vigilant against possible sting operations, amid reports that private agencies could be secretly recording Ministers’ conversations, meetings, and movements.
Deputy Chief Minister G. Parameshwara and Minister H.C. Balakrishna, who attended the Cabinet meeting on Tuesday (October 6, 2026), confirmed that Mr. Shivakumar, who also holds the Intelligence portfolio, had alerted the Ministers about possible sting operations.
“Since the Chief Minister holds the Intelligence portfolio, he cautioned us based on some information he had received,” Mr. Parameshwara told reporters.
Mr. Shivakumar is learnt to have raised the issue at the Cabinet meeting and shown the Ministers a “file” containing details of alleged ongoing sting operations. The file reportedly included the names of a few Ministers who were purportedly being targeted.
The Chief Minister is said to have advised the Ministers to exercise caution in the light of these purported developments. The Ministers were also reportedly advised to be cautious about meeting strangers privately or allowing themselves to be photographed with unfamiliar persons.
Political charge
Mr. Balakrishna, meanwhile, sought to link the alleged sting operations to Janata Dal (Secular) leader H.D. Kumaraswamy, accusing him of attempting to damage the Chief Minister’s political standing.
“Why did he not remember the NICE land issue and undertake a padayatra when Siddaramaiah was Chief Minister?” Mr. Balakrishna asked, referring to Mr. Kumaraswamy’s recent political campaigns against the Congress government.
The Minister alleged that Mr. Kumaraswamy had been using protests and padayatras since Mr. Shivakumar became Chief Minister in an attempt to undermine his position as a prominent Vokkaliga leader.
His remarks also referred to the State’s long history of political allegations involving purported CDs, pen drives and other forms of recorded material. About a decade ago, Mr. Kumaraswamy had claimed that he possessed CDs containing material relating to alleged corruption involving former Minister G. Janardhana Reddy, though the material was not subsequently made public.
The latest warning comes at a time when political activity is intensifying in Karnataka, with the major parties already positioning themselves for the 2028 Assembly elections.
This is not the first time Mr. Shivakumar has cautioned Congress leaders about possible action against them by investigating agencies. During the Enforcement Directorate searches involving the family members of Public Works Minister Satish Jarkiholi, he had claimed Congress MLAs and Ministers were under the agency’s scanner and urged party leaders to remain cautious.
The latest claims about alleged sting operations, however, have not been independently established.
Long history
The latest episode also revives Karnataka’s long history of political battles involving recorded conversations and purportedly incriminating material — from audio tapes in the 1980s to video CDs, sting operations, pen drives and, more recently, digitally recorded conversations and videos.
Such material has periodically been used as a political weapon, with allegations, counter-allegations, and demands for investigations often becoming part of electoral and intra-party battles.

briefs.headline: Karnataka High Court orders using ‘parenting time’ instead of ‘visitation’ in all child custody cases
briefs.deck: “Calling it ‘parenting time’ recognises a simple truth that no parent is a ‘visitor’ in the life of a child”
briefs.bodyText:
In a significant move aimed at reforming the language used in cases involving custody of a child between couples in conflict, the High Court of Karnataka has directed all family courts and courts dealing with guardians and wards (G&WC) cases henceforth to use the term “parenting time” instead of “visitation,” observing that no parent should be treated as a mere “visitor” in a child’s life.
Justice Lalitha Kanneganti, who was hearing a child custody case, issued the direction while pointing out that it is time for a small change in the language employed in judicial proceedings.
Pointing out that courts often use the word “visitation” to describe the time the child spends with a parent, who is a non-custodial parent, the court said that the word “visitation” is familiar, but “it carries an unfortunate suggestion that one parent is part of the child’s life while the other merely visits.”
“A child should not be made to understand the relationship through the word visitation, which is used for someone who arrives and leaves as a guest. Children read the conduct of adults and sometimes the words of courts to understand where they belong. Calling it parenting time recognises a simple truth that no parent is a visitor in the life of a child,” the court said.
Though a change in terminology does not decide questions of custody, when a court imposes restrictions on the access to the child, the word “parenting” is more humane, Justice Kanneganti said.
Also, the High Court directed the Registrar of General to issue a circular to all courts in this regard on the use of “parenting time” while also directing that even in the applications for child’s custody the word “parenting time” should be used instead of “visitation.”

briefs.headline: SIR surprise: In a first for Karnataka, more madams than sirs
briefs.deck: At 2.28 crore, Women Outnumber Men By 3.67 Lakh As On Oct 16
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Karnataka
’s electoral rolls have crossed a historic gender threshold, with women outnumbering men for the first time in the state’s electoral history, according to the latest figures released by the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO), Karnataka.
The electoral roll, as of Oct 16, lists 2.28 crore women against 2.25 crore men — a difference of nearly 3.7 lakh.Bengaluru: Karnataka’s electoral rolls have crossed a historic gender threshold, with women outnumbering men for the first time in the state’s electoral history, according to the latest figures released by the chief electoral officer (CEO) of Karnataka. The electoral roll, as of Oct 16, lists 2.28 crore women against 2.25 crore men — a difference of nearly 3.7 lakh.
The state has a total of 4.5 crore electors, including 2,860 third-gender voters. The milestone comes as the special intensive revision (SIR) enters its final stage, with the deadline for disposal of claims and objections set for Oct 22 and publication of the final electoral roll scheduled for Oct 27.
An analysis of historical Election Commission of India (ECI) data for Karnataka assembly election years shows that men outnumbered women in every year for which a separate gender-wise breakup was available, from 1962 through 2023. 
The 1957 report provided the total electorate but did not give separate male and female numbers, making 1962 the earliest year in the available series for which a comparison could be made.
Prof CM Lakshmana of the Population Research Centre at Institute for Social and Economic Change said the trend was surprising. “Based on Census data, the adult male-female ratio in recent years is nearly equal, but men outnumber women. So it is surprising to find more female electors than male. It would be difficult to make assessments without granular data,” he said.
The figures show that the shift is not uniform across the state. Women outnumber men in 25 of 34 districts listed in the release, while men remain ahead in nine. The largest female lead is in Mysuru, where women outnumber men by 49,416, followed by BBMP North, with a lead of 48,394. In contrast, men outnumber women by 42,269 in Bidar and 30,353 in Vijayapura. CEO Anbu Kumar V said the authorities had made efforts to ensure eligible voters could enrol. “We’ve made every effort to ensure no eligible voter misses an opportunity to get onto the rolls. We got 10 lakh new Form 6 applications, out of which more than 7.8 lakh were before Sept 23. All those applications need to be cleared; once all the applications are cleared, we’ll get a clear picture,” he said.
As of Oct 16, hearings had been completed in 43,63,459 of the 43,82,824 notices generated and delivered across Karnataka — 99.6% of the total. Hearings were pending in 19,365 cases. Gulbarga had the largest number of pending hearings, at 8,224, with 92.21% completed. Bengaluru Urban had 1,016 pending hearings and Belgaum 1,495.
Between June 16 and Oct 15, the CEO’s office received as many as 24,46,803 forms related to electoral roll claims, objections and updates. These included 10,07,392 Form 6 applications, 4,777 Form 6A applications, 1,55,109 Form 7 applications, and 12,79,525 Form 8 applications.
The final roll, due on Oct 27, will provide the next picture of Karnataka’s electorate after the claims-and-objections process is completed.

stories.headline: Serum Institute’s HPV vaccine Cervavac receives WHO prequalification

stories.bodyText:
Serum Institute of India’s recombinant Quadrivalent Human Papillomavirus vaccine (qHPV) vaccine Cervavac has received World Health Organization (WHO) prequalification.
The vaccine targets HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18. It is indicated for girls and boys aged 9 through 26 years. Inclusion on the WHO list of prequalified vaccines allows Cervavac to be procured by United Nations agencies, Serum Institute said.
The vaccine was developed in collaboration with the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) and the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC), along with the WHO-IARC (International Agency for Research on Cancer) and the Gates Foundation. It is the 32nd WHO prequalification for products/biologicals received by Serum Institute, the vaccine maker said.
“WHO prequalification of Cervavac is an important step in strengthening the global response to HPV. We are pleased to see this indigenously developed vaccine reach this achievement,” CEO Adar Poonawalla said.
Approved for use in India by DCGI
Cervavac has been approved for use in India by the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI). The vaccine is administered for the prevention of diseases caused by the four HPV types — prevention of anal cancer in boys and young men, and cervical, vulvar, vaginal, and anal cancers in girls and young women. It is also indicated in preventing genital warts, as applicable to the indicated population.
The vaccine is administered intramuscularly and available in 1-dose vials of 0.5 ml and 2-dose vials of 1.0 ml presentations.

stories.headline: As GST Council meets, tax experts say reforms must move beyond rates to processes and compliance
stories.deck: The GST Council will meet in New Delhi on October 8 for the first time after its meeting on September 3-4, 2025.
stories.bodyText:
With the Goods and Services Tax (GST) system having settled down, revenues remaining steady, and rates having been rationalised, tax experts across the board say the priority for the GST Council in its 57th meeting on October 8 should be on decisively easing the compliance burden for taxpayers.
The GST Council will meet in New Delhi on October 8 for the first time after its meeting on September 3-4, 2025, when it had introduced wide-ranging rate and slab changes. Sources in the Ministry of Finance have confirmed that the meeting will not deliberate on GST rates and will instead focus on a five-pronged effort to reform the tax system and its administration.
Tax analysts agree that this should be the priority of the Council.
Right time for reforms
The GST system turned nine years old on July 1, 2026. Through this time, the Council has met 56 times, has reformed the GST slabs, successfully implemented the 5-year compensation period to States, and the system has stabilised in terms of revenue.
“With high GST collections across the past few months, the GST Council in its next meeting scheduled on October 8, would be able to decide on several issues faced by businesses including relaxation of input tax credit restrictions, reducing complaints for service providers, providing faster refunds, etc, without being unduly worried about the impact of such measures on the GST collections,” MS Mani, Partner at Deloitte India, said.
The Hindu had reported on October 6 that the proposals by the Centre for the GST Council’s consideration would cover process reforms, structural reforms, ease of living and doing business, exports of services, and e-commerce. The final decisions will, however, be made clear only once the Council’s meeting concludes.
Several areas for improvement
“The most important process reforms will be allowing automatic and easy refunds especially to exporters, and preventing ITC accumulation, because these are economy wide effects on working capital for firms,” Rahul Ahluwalia, Founder Director of the Foundation for Economic Development said.
Prabhat Ranjan, Senior Director at Nexdigm, a business and tax consultancy, said that while rate rationalisation remains important, certainty of tax treatment can be as important as the rates themselves.
“A significant hidden cost of GST arises from interpretational uncertainty — whether on classification, input tax credit, valuation, place of supply or procedural requirements,” Mr. Ranjan explained. “When the same transaction can invite different positions across jurisdictions, businesses face not merely additional tax exposure but litigation costs, provisioning requirements, working-capital blockage and uncertainty in commercial decision-making.”
Technology to the rescue
Brijesh Agrawal, CEO of Busy Infotech, a company specialising in GST-related software services, said that the GST back-end system has become technologically sophisticated but everyday compliance remains complex for business owners.
“Key priorities should centre on consolidating tax slabs to a maximum of three [currently there are 6 slabs, including Zero/Nil, 0.25% and 3%], eliminating cess and overhauling Section 17(5) to allow unconditional credit on all verifiable business-to-business expenses,” Mr. Agrawal said.
At the moment, ordinary business costs are not entitled to input tax credits and so not only add to the costs of doing business but also potentially add to the price of the final product being sold.
The Hindu has learnt that the Centre is proposing a change in this regard, to allow ordinary business costs to also be included in the ambit of input tax credits.
Single registrations and audit
Another proposal that will be put up before the GST Council is to allow businesses to register in a single State and sell across the country instead of having to register their business in each of the States they want to sell in.
Nitin Vijaivergia, Partner, Price Waterhouse & Co further said that the proposed system of harmonising GST audits across multiple registrations would significantly ease the compliance burden on large taxpayers.
“A unified approach to issues that cuts across State lines would curb duplicative information requests and eliminate the risk of divergent conclusions on the same transaction,” Mr. Vijaivergia said.
“It would also equip tax authorities to deploy data analytics and risk parameters with precision, directing scrutiny where genuine risk lies,” he added. “For businesses, the dividend is clear: greater consistency, enhanced predictability and a leaner audit-related compliance cost.”

stories.headline: US seeks bids to exchange 17 million barrels of crude from strategic reserve
stories.deck: The United States plans to release 17 million barrels of crude oil from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve. This action aims to alleviate fuel price pressures amid disruptions caused by the war with Iran. The latest proposal is part of a broader international effort to stabilize energy markets announced in March. Despite earlier attempts yielding limited demand, the US continues to seek ways to…
stories.bodyText:
The United States is preparing to offer up to 17 million barrels of crude oil from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) as Washington steps up efforts to ease pressure on fuel prices amid disruptions caused by the war with Iran.
The US Department of Energy on Friday issued a request for proposals for the latest exchange, under which companies would borrow crude from the emergency stockpile and return oil at a later date, reported Reuters.
The move forms part of a broader international effort announced in March to stabilise energy markets after the conflict disrupted oil supplies and sent prices higher.
At the time, Washington committed to making 172 million barrels available from its strategic reserves as part of a coordinated International Energy Agency (IEA) initiative involving around 30 countries. The wider arrangement aimed to release 400 million barrels of emergency oil stocks worldwide.
However, an earlier attempt to offer the remaining barrels under the US commitment met with limited demand from energy companies.
In June, companies agreed to borrow only about 500,000 barrels after being required to return additional crude equivalent to premiums of up to 24 per cent, raising questions about the attractiveness of the exchange terms.
The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) is the country's emergency stockpile of crude oil, maintained to help cushion supply disruptions and stabilise energy markets during crises. Under an exchange programme, companies can borrow oil from the reserve and return it later, usually with additional barrels as a premium.
The latest proposal follows other attempts to increase global fuel supplies. Earlier this month, Trump reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to allow Russian diesel exports, with an initial 300,000 tonnes expected to be released. The move drew criticism from Ukraine and European leaders, who warned that easing restrictions could benefit Moscow financially.
Separately, G7 leaders announced on October 2 that they would implement a coordinated release of 100 million barrels of emergency oil stocks through the IEA over four months. The plan included an accelerated release of diesel supplies to address shortages in international markets.
Despite these measures, energy markets remain under strain. Brent crude was trading around $106 a barrel on Friday, with continuing attacks on Gulf shipping and disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz keeping supply concerns elevated.

briefs.headline: Property taxation needs structural reform
briefs.deck: The property tax performance of India’s municipal bodies has been poor — India’s cumulative property tax was 0.15-0.2% of its GDP
briefs.bodyText:
A robust property tax system is vital for India’s cities. Property tax is not just the most important own revenue source for India’s municipal bodies, it is also critical to bridge the gap in urban investment, as such investment depends on municipal creditworthiness. However, the property tax performance of India’s municipal bodies has been poor — India’s cumulative property tax was 0.15-0.2% of its GDP, whereas it was 0.6% in middle-income countries and 0.3% in low-income countries. Policy efforts have sought to improve the property tax performance of India’s municipal bodies through technology and process-based reforms recommended by successive Finance Commissions and national schemes such as the Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission and the Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation. Yet, tax outcomes remain sub-optimal. Why?
Two recent studies offer insights — a working paper on Chennai’s property tax by Nobel Laureate Esther Duflo and co-authors, and this writer’s research on Bengaluru, Pune and Ghaziabad’s property tax. Both studies found that technology and process-based reforms will keep yielding sub-optimal results unless backed by structural reforms. Firstly, Duflo and co-authors’ research in Chennai found that municipal human resources are a critical determinant of property tax outcomes. It also finds that a municipality’s own tax assessors achieve far better tax outcomes compared to assessors from outsourced firms. The research conducted across Bengaluru, Pune and Ghaziabad finds that in addition to the issue of municipal human resource deficits, two other structural issues — irregularity in the conduct of elections and poor financial reporting practices — also impact tax outcomes.
Stages of property tax
There are three life stages of property tax — enumeration (identification of properties and maintenance of property records along with property details), property valuation and tax assessment, and tax billing and collection.
Technology has been a popular policy solution for improving enumeration. GIS-based mapping using satellite imagery and drones have been increasingly deployed to identify properties. However, such mapping exercises need to be accompanied by physical inspections conducted by municipal tax assessors; they also need to be repeated at regular intervals. But a perennial shortage of municipal staff, lack of requisite skills, and inadequate capacity building plague India’s municipalities. While human resource outsourcing can be a substitute, its efficiency is limited, as municipal assessors leverage institutional memory in a way that outsourced assessors cannot.
For valuation, the most common policy recommendation has been the capital valuation process, wherein a property is valued as per its stamp duty-linked ‘circle rate’ which is set and revised by the State revenue department at regular intervals. But most municipal bodies follow a valuation method wherein the ‘base rate’ is defined in rupees per sq ft per month, which is set by the municipality. Hence, tax buoyancy is determined by revisions to this base rate. But such revisions are infrequent compared to revisions in the stamp duty-linked circle rate. It was found that ‘base rate’ revisions did not take place across Bengaluru, Pune and Ghaziabad when there were no elected municipal councils. The link between municipal elections and tax performance is clear, at least for these three corporations. As delayed municipal elections are common, so is infrequent ‘base rate’ revision and lack of tax buoyancy.
Finally, for tax collections to be robust, collection efficiency needs to be strong. While extant recommendations include the adoption of both online collection as well as outsourcing the collection to external vendors, efficiency remains poor. Even more concerning is the difficulty in arriving at credible collection efficiency estimates due to the absence of properly maintained financial accounts.
To sum up, technology and process-based reforms are not enough for improving tax outcomes. Structural reforms encompassing more human resources, timely elections, and publicly available financial data play very important roles. It is high time that policy interventions broaden their focus to structural reforms for all aspects of urban governance and finance, including property tax.
Debarpita Roy is Lead-Research at the Centre for Public Policy on Housing and Habitat, NIUA, New Delhi. The views are personal.

briefs.headline: Failure to finalise US trade deal may hurt India, but new FTAs can cushion tariff blow: RBI chief
briefs.deck: The diversification of India’s export markets and products as another buffer against a potential tariff shock.
briefs.bodyText:
A failure to finalise a trade deal between India and the U.S. could have “some negative impact” on the Indian economy, but a string of recent trade agreements and diversification of exports could cushion the fallout from any additional U.S. tariffs, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Sanjay Malhotra said on Wednesday.
“We do not know, first of all, which sectors will be impacted and to what extent these tariffs are going to be applied. So, it is premature. But it will obviously have some negative impact,” Mr. Malhotra said in response to a question from The Hindu.
However, India’s recent trade agreements, including those already operationalised and those in the pipeline, would help mitigate the impact, he said.
The governor also pointed to the diversification of India’s export markets and products as another buffer against a potential tariff shock.
“All these will mitigate the effect if, in case, there is an additional tariff on some of the sectors,” he said.
His comments come amid a prolonged deadlock in India-US trade negotiations. Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said earlier this week that offering any further concessions to the U.S. would be difficult and that the talks had reached a “plateau”, with Washington reportedly seeking additional concessions.
The negotiations have assumed greater significance following the passage by the U.S. Congress in September of the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which gives President Donald Trump powers to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries, including India, over purchases of Russian and Iranian oil and gas. Mr. Trump has signed the legislation, but the additional tariffs have not been imposed, with the trade negotiations still underway.
Repo hike unlikely to derail credit growth
Mr. Malhotra also said the RBI’s 25-basis-point repo rate increase was unlikely to have an immediate impact on bank credit growth, as monetary policy transmission typically takes several quarters.
The rate hike will eventually push up borrowing costs as banks transmit the higher policy rate to lending rates, but the impact on credit growth is expected to emerge with a lag.

briefs.bodyText:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday (October 7, 2026) decided to ask the Union government why millions of passengers with disabilities continue to face humiliation, barriers, broken equipment, and digital exclusion in one of the world’s fastest growing aviation markets.
A three-judge Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant issued formal notice to the Ministry of Civil Aviation, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation, the Airports Authority of India, the Central Industrial Security Force, and the Digi Yatra Foundation on a petition filed by Turab Chimthanawala, a company secretary and advocate based in Mumbai, who suffers a benchmark disability called Leber’s Congenital Amaurosis.
Advocate Ashutosh Senger, for Mr. Chimthanawala, submitted that India was presently the third-largest aviation market globally, with annual passenger traffic exceeding 350 million passengers. Yet, persons with disabilities (PwD) face denial of accessible aviation infrastructure and services, restricting their fundamental right to travel independently and with dignity.
“Domestic passenger traffic has consistently grown at approximately 10-12% annually over the past decade. Even based on the conservative estimate of 2.21% disability prevalence recorded in the Census of 2011, this translates to over seven million air passengers with disabilities annually...The magnitude of affected persons underscores the systemic and national scale of the accessibility failure,” Mr. Senger submitted.
The petition referred to recent media reports of a wheelchair-dependent passenger who was allegedly offloaded in Delhi while connecting from a Frankfurt flight.
The plea highlighted a systemic and nationwide failure of non-implementation of accessibility across all stages of air travel, including booking, web-check-in, airport entry and navigation, counter check-in, security screening, Digi Yatra processing, immigration, boarding, in-flight services, and arrival assistance.
These include instances of visually handicapped passengers routinely forced into wheelchairs or being frequently compelled to use specialised ambulifts even when they can safely use regular staircases. Crucial personal assistive equipment, including specialised battery-operated wheelchairs, are found regularly damaged, misplaced, or outright denied loading into aircraft holds by ground handling staff. In-flight systems fail to incorporate accessibility settings, leaving visually handicapped passengers unable to call cabin crew or access basic safety information on foreign scheduled air transport services.
Silent airports fail to provide accessible alternative modes of communication for PwD, including real-time audio notifications, visual alerts, or WhatsApp updates, the petition said.
Besides, airline mobile applications and booking websites systematically fail to support screen readers, lack compatible payment gateways for assistive technology, and omit mandatory options to disclose disability-related assistance requirements during check-in.
Further, airlines do not provide dedicated, clearly identifiable feedback or grievance mechanisms for reporting accessibility barriers, forcing disabled travelers into generic customer support queues where specific accessibility issues go unaddressed.
“Accessibility is not merely a statutory entitlement but a fundamental right flowing from the guarantee of equality, dignity, and freedom of movement, and imposes a non-derogable obligation upon the state and its instrumentalities to ensure that public infrastructure and services are usable by PwDs on an equal basis with others,” the petition said.

briefs.headline: Foreign airlines grouping urges for alternatives to flight cuts at Mumbai airport
briefs.deck: IATA says MIAL and carriers must work on transition plan to protect international connectivity to Mumbai Metropolitan Region
briefs.bodyText:
The International Air Transport Association (IATA), the global airline industry body, has called for a consultative approach between Adani-owned Mumbai International Airport Ltd. (MIAL) and airlines to ensure that the redevelopment of Terminal 1 does not undermine international connectivity to the Mumbai Metropolitan Region (MMR).
IATA also urged stakeholders to explore alternatives to flight cuts and other capacity reductions.
Welcoming the Ministry of Civil Aviation’s (MoCA) intervention asking MIAL to defer its proposed 33% reduction in flight operations from October 26, IATA said the decision to re-engage with stakeholders offered an opportunity to develop a collaborative transition plan.
“The discussion now provides an opportunity for stakeholders using the airport to review the underlying capacity requirements, understand the basis of any proposed capacity reduction, examine alternatives that may mitigate such reductions, and work collaboratively on a transition plan that protects passenger interests, airline operations and the international connectivity of the Mumbai Metropolitan Region,” IATA said in a statement.
IATA said any significant reduction in airport capacity should be backed by a transparent demand-capacity assessment, meaningful consultation with affected airlines and adequate time to put workable transition arrangements in place.
MIAL had proposed reducing international flight operations at Mumbai airport’s Terminal 2 by 33% while Terminal 1 undergoes redevelopment. The affected flights were to be shifted to Navi Mumbai International Airport, which is also operated by the Adani group. Domestic flights currently operating from T1 would subsequently be moved to T2.
International airlines have raised concerns over the impact on flight schedules and connectivity, as well as the operational challenges and additional costs of splitting their operations between two airports serving the same metropolitan region.

briefs.headline: RBI to allow inter-operability among account aggregators; integrate bank deposits with CAS
briefs.deck: “Account aggregator will give you an overview of all your financial assets at one view.” Mr. Malhotra
briefs.bodyText:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will enable interoperability among Non-Banking Finance Company account aggregators (NBFC-AAs), allowing individuals to access information on their financial assets through a single platform.
The framework will be implemented by December 31, 2026, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said while announcing additional measures alongside the monetary policy statement.
The RBI will also facilitate Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)-regulated depositories to include bank deposit information in consolidated account statements (CAS), Mr. Malhotra said.
“Account aggregator will give you an overview of all your financial assets,” he said, noting that information is currently fragmented across about 15 AAs. Interoperability would allow the information to be integrated, giving individuals a consolidated view of their financial assets.
With customer consent, the data could also be accessed by insurance brokers, asset managers and investment advisers, enabling them to offer more informed financial advice, he said.
Mr. Malhotra said CAS currently does not include bank deposits, leaving a significant gap in an individual’s consolidated financial picture. The RBI will facilitate the inclusion of deposit information from banks already onboarded on the system, with other banks to be brought in over time.
The move is also expected to help in tracking dormant bank deposits, particularly after the death of an account holder. A consolidated view of financial assets could make it easier for families to identify such assets, Mr. Malhotra said.
The interoperability push could also strengthen the use of financial data for credit assessment. Umesh Revankar, executive vice-chairman of Shriram Finance Ltd, said the reform would facilitate easier sharing of financial information, deepen cash-flow-based underwriting and bring more first-time borrowers into formal credit.
“From this position of strength, we will keep driving credit inclusion deeper into semi-urban and rural India, for the small truck operator, the rural entrepreneur and the MSME borrower who power India’s growth,” Mr. Revankar said.

briefs.headline: Why is the price of rice rising across the country? | Explained
briefs.deck: The central government issued an advisory to States asking farmers to shift to short-duration crops or less-water-intensive crops like pulses and millets. In June, Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said: “Changing crop strategy in rain-fed areas has become the need of the hour”
briefs.bodyText:
The story so far: The price of rice, the staple of most Indian meals, especially in South India, has gone up suddenly. A 26-kilogram bag of fine rice that used to retail at ₹1,800 per bag, or about ₹70 per kilogram, is now retailing for ₹2,150 per bag, or about ₹82 per kg.
Nationally, the area under rice cultivation for Kharif (monsoon crop) has dropped from 449.18 lakh hectares in 2025-26 to 433.62 lakh hectares. A drop of 3.46% in area sown, according to data from the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare. The drop in area under rice cultivation is linked to the forecast of a ‘below normal monsoon’ by the India Meteorological Department in May this year that factored in the likely impact of ‘El Niño’. The periodic climate pattern of warming of the Pacific Ocean that affects trade winds and the Indian monsoon. The central government issued an advisory to States asking farmers to shift to short-duration crops or less-water-intensive crops like pulses and millets. In June, Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan, after a meeting with State government officials, research bodies, IMD and others, said: “Changing crop strategy in rain-fed areas has become the need of the hour”.

briefs.headline: Aragen Life Sciences begins operations at a high-potency development manufacturing platform in Hyderabad
briefs.bodyText:
IPO-bound contract research, development and manufacturing organisation (CRDMO) Aragen Life Sciences has begun operations at Aragen OneHP, a high-potency development and manufacturing platform at its Nacharam campus in Hyderabad.
Aragen OneHP spans around 15,000 sq ft and operates one manufacturing line with a designed capacity of 500-600 kg of active pharmaceutical ingredient per year. It can support highly potent compounds, including cytotoxic molecules and targeted oncology therapies. The facility will also lay the foundation for future expansion into advanced modalities such as antibody-drug conjugates and peptide-drug conjugates, the company said on Wednesday (October 7, 2026).
For customers, the platform will provide an integrated pathway from milligram-scale discovery through process development and multi-kilogram cGMP manufacturing.
Aragen said the platform is its most recent addition as part of a programme to new capabilities. It has incurred more than ₹1000 crore capital expenditure over three years ended March 2026 on building capability across small molecules and biologics. Installed small-molecule capacity stood at 364 KL across Hyderabad and Visakhapatnam as of March 31, 2026.
“With OneHP, we are bringing discovery, development and cGMP manufacturing for highly potent molecules onto a more integrated platform,” said Aniel Khubchandani, CEO-Small Molecules-CDMO.
The company operates a network of research and development as well as manufacturing facilities in Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Visakhapatnam and Pune in India and Morgan Hill, California, in the U.S., with a team of 4,362 employees as of March 31, 2026.
Aragen had in August filed Draft Red Herring Prospectus (DRHP) with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) for an initial public offering (IPO) comprising a fresh issue of ₹800 crore and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 27,329,192 equity shares, with a face value of ₹10 each, by existing selling shareholders.

stories.headline: Under pressure and on the move: India coach flags mental fatigue in camp
stories.deck: Indian cricketers have had a busy couple of months, playing several bilateral series as well as competing at the Asian Games in Japan.
stories.bodyText:
India's fast bowling coach 
Morne Morkel
 on Friday praised the bowlers for continuing to deliver for the team despite the “mental fatigue” caused by a packed schedule.
Indian cricketers have had a busy couple of months, playing several bilateral series as well as competing at the Asian Games in Japan.
“I read everything that's written on social media. One thing that we sometimes forget is that mental fatigue plays a big part. We have to manage that and you have to be smart with it. If you look at this T20 side, some of the players went for the Asian Games, and then went straight into a full series now (vs the West Indies),” Morkel said on the eve of the fifth T20I in Bengaluru.
“Then they had to fly off to Delhi for a presentation there (meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi) and back here in the morning. And, now, we have to get them ready for a game. So, that is the reality and these guys are also human,” he added.
Morkel stressed that players need enough time to recover between matches to perform at their best.
“And for me, your execution and your skills will be better when you've recovered well, when you've slept well, and once you've mentally refreshed and that is a challenge. We're going to fly now to New Zealand. It's a jam-packed schedule there as well.”
With another busy schedule ahead, the former South African fast bowler urged people to be measured in their criticism of the team's bowling performances.
“And that is sometimes a tricky thing. So, I've got a lot of respect for these guys, with the performances that they are at the moment producing for Team India, with the schedule we have.
“You know, and that's why I sometimes think we can allow them to make a mistake and allow them to have an off game and not be on them, because of the mental load and expectation on these players,” he added.

stories.headline: ‘I am not pushed enough’: National record holder Vithya sets sights on sub-54 run next
stories.deck: The 28-year-old says she doesn’t get the fanfare surrounding her Asian Games performance, where she bagged three medals for India; coach Nehpal wants her to perform well in the Beijing World athletics championships next year
stories.bodyText:
Vithya Ramraj still cannot understand the hype surrounding her.
The 28-year-old, who emerged as one of India’s standout performers at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, returned with three medals and a National record in the 400m hurdles, breaking P.T. Usha’s 42-year-old mark.
“In the last Asian Games (2023) in Hangzhou, I won three medals. I don’t know why I became popular this time,” she told select media at a function organised by jewellery brand Tanishq (Anna Nagar) on Wednesday.
She might sound modest, but her performance speaks for itself. She played the anchor role brilliantly to help India win the gold medal in the women’s 4x400m relay, ran a brilliant race to break Usha’s long-standing record in the 400m hurdles (bronze) and did well to guide India to a silver in the 4x400m mixed relay.
Though Vithya is happy to have won bronze in the 400m hurdles at the Games while breaking the National record (54.75s), the athlete and her personal coach, Nehpal Singh, felt she should focus on running sub-54 next.
“My coach is not happy with my timing in the 400m hurdles at the Games in Japan. In India, I am not pushed enough... hence, I am not able to go sub-54. I will work harder and try to achieve the timing my coach has demanded of me,” said Vithya.
When asked about the facilities at the cruise ship where the team stayed in Japan, Vithya replied: “I’ve lived in a room with 20 members. We lived like that for six years. There were no reservations during travel for competitions. My coach (Nehpal) said, ‘Don’t care about anything. Just go and run the race.’”
In all probability, Vithya will make her debut at the World athletics championships next year in Beijing. “I want Vithya to make it to the final. That’s the target,” said Nehpal.
According to Vithya, the key to her success at the Asian Games was the good sleep she had in Spala (Poland), where she trained prior to the Games. “I slept for 10 hours in those three months. That was what brought my performance,” she said.
She will be keen to maintain the sleep cycle to achieve higher dreams.

stories.headline: The journey from a promising partnership to a world-class combination for Manush and Diya
stories.deck: For Indian table tennis, it was the fourth medal at the Asian Games and ensured that the sport had a podium finish for a third consecutive time
stories.bodyText:
For four days in early September, Manush Shah travelled to Mumbai, the hometown of his mixed doubles partner Diya Chitale for a relatively simple job. Train.
There were no selection meetings to worry about, no administrative developments to follow, no uncertainty over who would be around the Indian table tennis team. In Mumbai, the pair could concentrate on the one thing that had brought them together in the first place — making their partnership work.
Those four days would prove valuable when they eventually arrived in Aichi-Nagoya.
The sixth-seeded Indian pair went on to win a bronze medal at the Asian Games, beating Hong Kong’s third-seeded Wong Chun Ting and Doo Hoi Kem in the quarterfinals before losing to eventual silver medallists Wong Chuqin and Sun Yingsha of China in the semifinals.
For Indian table tennis, the medal was significant. It was the fourth at the Asian Games and ensured that the sport had a podium finish at a third successive edition of the continental extravaganza.
For Manush and Diya, though, the bronze represented something more personal. It was the reward for a partnership that had steadily climbed the international ladder and, in the process, had learnt to complement two very different games.
It was also an affirmation that, amid a turbulent build-up, they had managed to keep the noise away from the table.
When Diya spoke about going into her second Asian Games, she did not need to be reminded of the difference between a regular international tournament and a multi-sport event. Her first Asian Games, in Hangzhou three years ago, had given her that perspective.
“Going into my second Asian Games, I think the first one gave me a lot of experience and exposure,” Diya told The Hindu before leaving for Japan. “Representing the country at a multi-sport event is a very different feeling. It was a great experience in 2023, and I wanted to carry that experience forward.” But there was a difference this time. The expectations were higher. Diya and Manush were no longer simply an emerging combination hoping to make an impression. They had become one of India’s principal medal contenders, their progress reflected by a place among the world’s top-eight pairs at the 2025 WTT Finals, the season-ending event reserved for the leading performers of the year.
“We have been doing really well in doubles,” Diya had said ahead of the Games. “Me and Manush have been doing really, really well for the last two or three years. When we started, our graph has gone up a lot.”
That graph eventually took them to an Asian Games podium. The bronze did not arrive out of nowhere. Over the preceding seasons, the pair had learnt the demands of international mixed doubles, where the rhythm and speed of a rally can differ considerably from men’s doubles.
Manush described the distinction in simple terms. “In men’s doubles, you expect power from the opponents. The ball really travels and you expect good quality, so you don’t have to manage the front-and-back movement as much,” he said.
“In mixed doubles, it is the opposite. The front-and-back movement becomes really important because the woman on the opposing pair may not be as powerful. They try to play quickly, so the ball can be a little slower and you have to make faster adjustments with your footwork.” That difference requires more than just technical ability. It requires trust. “In mixed doubles, Diya is the one with the control and I try to finish the point,” Manush said. “If this works out, then we are already one step ahead of the opponent. That is what the goal is all about in doubles.” The quarterfinal against Hong Kong was evidence of that equation working when it mattered.
India’s table tennis contingent had not arrived at Aichi-Nagoya without precedent. In 2018, the men’s team won a historic bronze and Sharath Kamal and Manika Batra added another bronze in mixed doubles. In Hangzhou, Ayhika Mukherjee and Sutirtha Mukherjee produced a surprise run to the women’s doubles bronze. Manush and Diya’s medal therefore extended the sequence of Indian table tennis appearing on the Asian Games podium. Yet it carried a different weight.
Unlike the Hangzhou women’s doubles bronze, which came as a surprise, this was a medal India had begun to expect from the pair. Their qualification for the WTT Finals in 2025 had placed them among the world’s leading combinations, while their performances over the preceding couple of seasons had made them a credible medal proposition.
“Since two or three years, we have been doing really well,” Diya had said. “We understand each other’s game better now. We know each other’s strengths and weaknesses.”
That understanding had been tested against the world’s best. “We have played a lot of top pairs over the years,” she said. “We have beaten a top Japanese pair and qualified for the WTT Finals, where the top eight pairs in the world play. All these experiences put together have helped us reach where we are today.”
The Asian Games simply provided the biggest stage yet on which that accumulated experience had to translate into a result. And it did. The achievement becomes more significant when the build-up to the Asian Games is considered. Indian table tennis spent much of the preceding months dealing with issues away from the playing arena.
The selection controversy surrounding Manika Batra had cast a shadow over the process after she was left out of the Asian Games squad for failing to meet the prescribed selection criteria. The episode led to questions about the transparency of the selection system and public exchanges between the paddler and the federation.
Then, in August, the Sports Ministry suspended the recognition of the Table Tennis Federation of India as the National Sports Federation for table tennis, citing a series of administrative and governance issues. The turmoil had consequences beyond the boardroom.
Massimo Costantini’s tenure as India’s foreign expert had expired on May 15, and the uncertainty surrounding the federation meant his continuation with the national set-up was delayed. The Italian eventually joined the Indian contingent in Japan only a week before the Asian Games. Against that backdrop, Manush and Diya had little choice but to concentrate on what they could control.
Rising expectations
There was no luxury of an extended camp dedicated exclusively to the mixed doubles combination. The international calendar rarely allows it. But the partnership had already developed enough understanding to make those sessions count.
Diya was aware before the Games that expectations would follow them. The pair’s rise had ensured that. “Pressure is always going to be there,” she had said. “There will always be some expectations and some pressure. But what is important is that we gave our best and are happy with the way it progressed.” That attitude became particularly relevant in the quarterfinal. A defeat would have meant another near-miss for Indian table tennis. A victory would guarantee at least a bronze. Manush and Diya delivered. The win over Wong and Doo, seeded third, confirmed the medal and effectively transformed their status from contenders to medallists. The bronze was secure.
While Manush has come a long way since starting to train under Shailesh Gosain’s watchful eyes in Vadodara, Diya has been coached by Sachin Shetty ever since she took up the sport more than a decade and a half ago. Since their junior days, Olympic Gold Quest has been supporting the duo’s journey towards excellence in the international circuit. Government support has also reduced some of the financial pressure on athletes and their families. “With so many government schemes, the Government helps a lot with the TOPS scheme,” Diya said. “Of course, that also relieves the financial pressure on the parents.” That support becomes especially relevant when an athlete is required to travel extensively, train continuously and compete against the world’s best.
By the time Diya and Manush stepped onto the Asian Games arena, they were carrying the work of that entire ecosystem with them. More than just a bronze. The significance of the medal extends beyond the result of one quarterfinal and one semifinal.
It means India has now won table tennis medals at three consecutive Asian Games. It means the country has a established mixed doubles combination capable of competing with the best in Asia. And it confirms that Manush and Diya’s journey from promising partnership to world-class combination has been real. Their qualification for the 2025 WTT Finals had already indicated where they belonged. The Asian Games provided a different kind of test — one where the draw, the occasion and the weight of expectations all mattered.
They responded by beating the third seeds and securing India’s only table tennis medal at the Games. The loss to the Chinese pair in the semifinal did not diminish what had been achieved. If anything, it reinforced the progression.
Three years earlier, Diya had entered her first Asian Games looking for experience and exposure while Manush had endured the disappointment of being one point away from a medal in men’s doubles. This time they went for a medal.
“We went into the Asian Games aiming for a medal,” Diya said. “And we are thrilled that we have achieved the objective and have brought that medal home”.
